Calculate $$
\displaystyle {∮}_{∂D}3y\,dx+2x\,dy,
$$ where $D$ is the annular region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=3y$ and $Q(x,y)=2x.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=3,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=2.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}3y\,dx+2x\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2-3)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}-1\,\text{d}A \\  & =-{∬}_{D}\,\text{d}A \\  & =-\text{Area}(D) \\  & =-(\pi \cdot {3}^{2}-\pi \cdot {1}^{2}) \\  & =-(9\pi -\pi ) \\  & =-8\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Our simple, piecewise-smooth, closed path $C$ is positively oriented and  

$$
\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y}=1-0=1.
$$

So, according to Green's theorem, we can write the area of the region $D$ enclosed by the curve $C$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Area}(D) & ={∬}_{D}\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

  

Substituting $P(x,y)=0$ and $Q(x,y)=x,$ we get

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,\text{d}x+Q\,\text{d}y={∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y.
$$

 

The derivatives of ${r}_{1}(t)$ and ${r}_{2}(t)$ are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{C}_{1}:\, & {r}_{1}^{′}(t)=5{t}^{4}\,i+4{t}^{3}\,j \\ {C}_{2}:\, & {r}_{2}^{′}(t)=-i\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write our line integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{C}x\,\text{d}y & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}\cup {C}_{2}}x\,dy \\  & ={∮}_{{C}_{1}}x\,dy+{∮}_{{C}_{2}}x\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{5}\cdot 4{t}^{3}\,\text{d}t+{\int }_{-1}^{1}(-t)\cdot 0\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{1}{t}^{8}\,\text{d}t-0 \\  & =4[\frac{{t}^{9}}{9}]_{-1}^{1} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{2}{9} \\  & =\frac{8}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=-{x}^{4}y-\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}{y}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=x{y}^{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}{y}^{2}.$ So,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=-{x}^{4}-{x}^{2}{y}^{2},\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}={y}^{4}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}-({x}^{4}y+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{2}{y}^{3})\,dx+(x{y}^{4}+\frac{1}{3}{x}^{3}{y}^{2})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{4}+{x}^{2}{y}^{2}-(-{x}^{4}-{x}^{2}{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{x}^{4}+2{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+{y}^{4}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in polar coordinates as 

$$
Δ={(r,\theta )\,:\,1\le r\le 3,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi }.
$$

Recall that the change of variables formula for polar coordinates gives

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dA={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta .
$$

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}((r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}+(r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )^{2})^{2}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{4}({cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )^{2}\cdot r\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{5}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta {\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{5}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi {\int }_{1}^{3}{r}^{5}\,\text{d}r \\  & =2\pi \cdot {\frac{1}{6}{r}^{6}|}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{\pi }{3}\cdot ({3}^{6}-{1}^{6}) \\  & =\frac{728\pi }{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$
where $D$ is the region shown above.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Let $C$ be a positively oriented, piecewise-smooth, simple closed curve in the plane, and let $D$ be the region bounded by $C.$ If $P$ and $Q$ have continuous first partial derivatives on an open region containing $D,$ then Green's theorem states that

$$
{∮}_{C}P\,dx+Q\,dy={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Green's theorem can be extended to include regions containing holes. In such cases, we can apply Green's theorem in the same way as before.

We have that $P(x,y)=x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3}$ and $Q(x,y)=2{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3}.$ Therefore,

$$
\frac{∂P}{∂y}=2xy,\,\frac{∂Q}{∂x}=4xy.
$$

Therefore, applying Green's theorem, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∮}_{∂D}(x{y}^{2}+{x}^{3})\,dx+(2{x}^{2}y-{y}^{3})\,dy & ={∬}_{D}(\frac{∂Q}{∂x}-\frac{∂P}{∂y})\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}4xy-2xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

The region $D$ can be represented in Cartesian coordinates as ${Δ}_{1}∖{Δ}_{2},$ where

- ${Δ}_{1}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-2\le x\le 2,-1\le y\le 2\}$ is the region enclosed by the outer curve, and

- ${Δ}_{2}=\{(x,y)\,:\,-1\le x\le 1,0\le y\le 1\}$ is the region enclosed by the inner curve.

Therefore, our double integral becomes

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2xy\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{{Δ}_{1}}2xy\,\text{d}A-{∬}_{{Δ}_{2}}2xy\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-2}^{2}2xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-1}^{1}2xy\,\text{d}x\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{-1}^{2}y\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{-1}^{1}2x\,\text{d}x{\int }_{0}^{1}y\,\text{d}y \\  & ={x}^{2}\,{|}_{-2}^{2}\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\,{|}_{-1}^{2}-{x}^{2}\,{|}_{-1}^{1}\cdot \frac{{y}^{2}}{2}\,{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(4-4)\cdot (2-\frac{1}{2})-(1-1)\cdot (\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =0\cdot \frac{3}{2}-0\cdot \frac{1}{2} \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
The level curves of the function $f(x,y)=\frac{x+y}{x}$ are given by $f(x,y)=c.$ Which of the following statements are true?

Select all that apply.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Setting $f(x,y)=c$ gives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{x+y}{x} & =c \\ x+y & =cx \\ y & =(c-1)x\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore:

- If $c=-1,$ the level curve is the line $y=-2x,$ excluding the origin. So, “$c=-1$ gives the $x$-axis, excluding the origin” is false.

- If $c=0,$ the level curve is the line $y=-x,$ excluding the origin. So, “$c=0$ gives the $y$-axis, excluding the origin” is false.

- If $c=1,$ the level curve is $y=0,$ which is the $x$-axis (excluding the origin). So, “$c=1$ gives the line $y=x,$ excluding the origin” is false.

So, the correct answer is "None of the listed".

$$

Therefore:

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-1}^{5}\boxed{}\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.
$$

What is the missing expression?
question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ with parametrization $r(u,v)$ for $(u,v)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{S}F\cdot n\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A.
$$

Using the parametrization, where $x=u$ and $y=v,$ our surface can be parameterized as

$$
r(u,v)=⟨u,\,v,\,2u-4v⟩
$$

over the domain 

$$
D=\{(u,v)\,:\,-2\le u\le 0,\,-1\le v\le 5\}.
$$

We now compute the tangent vectors to the grid curves:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂u},\,\frac{∂y}{∂u},\,\frac{∂z}{∂u}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂u}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂u}(2u-4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨1,\,0,\,2⟩ \\ {r}_{v}^{′} & =⟨\frac{∂x}{∂v},\,\frac{∂y}{∂v},\,\frac{∂z}{∂v}⟩ \\  & =⟨\frac{∂}{∂v}(u),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(v),\,\frac{∂}{∂v}(2u-4v)⟩ \\  & =⟨0,\,1,\,-4⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Now, the fundamental vector product is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′} & =\begin{vmatrix}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -4\end{vmatrix} \\  & =⟨\begin{vmatrix}0 & 2 \\ 1 & -4\end{vmatrix},\,-\begin{vmatrix}1 & 2 \\ 0 & -4\end{vmatrix},\,\begin{vmatrix}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{vmatrix}⟩ \\  & =⟨-2,\,4,\,1⟩.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the coordinate expressions of $r(u,v)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v)) & =⟨z+x,\,y+2z,\,x-4y⟩{|}_{x=u,\,\,y=v,\,\,z=2u-4v} \\  & =⟨2u-4v+u,\,v+2(2u-4v),\,u-4v⟩ \\  & =⟨3u-4v,\,4u-7v,\,u-4v⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we calculate the dot product of $F$ and ${r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′}) & =⟨3u-4v,\,4u-7v,\,u-4v⟩\cdot ⟨-2,\,4,\,1⟩ \\  & =(3u-4v)\cdot (-2)+(4u-7v)\cdot 4+(u-4v)\cdot 1 \\  & =-6u+8v+16u-28v+u-4v \\  & =11u-24v.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨z+x,\,y+2z,\,x-4y⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}F(r(u,v))\cdot ({r}_{u}^{′}\times {r}_{v}^{′})\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(11u-24v)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-2}^{0}{\int }_{-1}^{5}(11u-24v)\,\text{d}v\,\text{d}u.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
For a surface $S$ given by $z=g(x,y)$ for $(x,y)\in D,$ the flux of a vector field $F(x,y,z)=⟨P,\,Q,\,R⟩$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}F\cdot \text{d}S={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A.
$$

We first compute the partial derivatives of the graph $z=g(x,y):$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂g}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-2x)=-2 \\ \frac{∂g}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-2x)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we substitute the equation $z=g(x,y)$ into $F(x,y,z):$

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x,y,g(x,y)) & =⟨y,\,x+z,\,z+2x⟩{|}_{z=y-2x} \\  & =⟨y,\,x+(y-2x),\,y-2x+2x⟩ \\  & =⟨\underbrace{y}_{P},\,\underbrace{y-x}_{Q},\,\underbrace{y}_{R}⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can evaluate our surface integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}⟨y,\,x+z,\,z+2x⟩\cdot \text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}(-P\frac{∂g}{∂x}-Q\frac{∂g}{∂y}+R)\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(-y\cdot (-2)-(y-x)\cdot (1)+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2y-y+x+y)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(2y+x)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(2y+x)\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{[{y}^{2}+xy]}_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}(1+x)\,\text{d}x \\  & ={[x+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2}]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =2+2-1-\frac{1}{2} \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem: Let $f(x,y)=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}),$ where $x=t{e}^{s}$ and $y=t{e}^{-s}.$ Calculate $\frac{∂f}{∂t}.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
![](images/11/118759b163a4410f66d5855d7b7b1fd9c2ee4be585e778a759997036bd95f765.png)

The chain rule for a multivariable function $f(x,y)$ with two independent variables $s$ and $t,$ where $x=x(s,t)$ and $y=y(s,t),$ can be expressed as follows:

$$
\frac{∂f}{∂t}=\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t}
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives of $f$ with respect to $x$ and $y:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}=\frac{2x}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}},\,\frac{∂f}{∂y}=\frac{2y}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Writing the above results in terms of $s$ and $t,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{2(t{e}^{s})}{(t{e}^{s})^{2}+(t{e}^{-s})^{2}}=\frac{2{e}^{s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}, \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{2(t{e}^{-s})}{(t{e}^{s})^{2}+(t{e}^{-s})^{2}}=\frac{2{e}^{-s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}.\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we take the derivatives of $x$ and $y$ with respect to $t,$ and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂x}{∂t} & ={e}^{s}, \\ \frac{∂y}{∂t} & ={e}^{-s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, substituting all of our derivatives into the multivariable chain rule, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂t} & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\cdot \frac{∂x}{∂t}+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\cdot \frac{∂y}{∂t} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}\cdot {e}^{s}+\frac{2{e}^{-s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}\cdot {e}^{-s} \\  & =\frac{2{e}^{2s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}+\frac{2{e}^{-2s}}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})} \\  & =\frac{2({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})}{t({e}^{2s}+{e}^{-2s})} \\  & =\frac{2}{t}.\end{aligned}
$$

question.:question/problem:
Determine the domain of the vector field $F$ on ${R}^{2},$ given by

$$
F(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4}\right)\,i+\frac{xy}{x-1}\,j\,.
$$
question.:question/worked-solution:
The function $F$ can be expressed in terms of its components $P(x,y)$ and $Q(x,y)$ as

$$
F(x,y)=P(x,y)\,i+Q(x,y)\,j,
$$

where

$$
P(x,y)=\operatorname{arctan}⁡\left(\frac{1}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4}\right),\,Q(x,y)=\frac{xy}{x-1}.
$$

We first find the domain of each component function. Then, we compute their intersection to find the domain of $F:$

- The function $P(x,y)$ is defined everywhere other than when the denominator vanishes. To find where the denominator vanishes, we set it equal to zero and solve:

$$
{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}-4=0\,⟹\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4.
$$

Therefore, the domain of $P$ is given by

$$
{D}_{1}={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 4}.
$$

- The function $Q(x,y)$ is defined everywhere other than when the denominator vanishes. To find where the denominator vanishes, we set it equal to zero and solve:

$$
x-1=0\,⟹\,x=1
$$

Therefore, the domain of $Q$ is given by

$$
{D}_{2}={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,x\ne 1}.
$$

Finally, the domain $D$ of $F$ is given by

$$
D={D}_{1}\cap {D}_{2}={(x,y)\in {R}^{2}\,|\,{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}\ne 4,\,x\ne 1}\,.
$$

question.:question/problem: For which of the following vector fields is $f(x,y)=x\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1)$ a potential function?
question.:question/worked-solution:
A vector field $F$ is conservative if it is the gradient of a scalar function $f.$ That is, there exists a function $f$ such that $F=∇f.$ The function $f$ is called a potential function for $F.$

To compute the vector field associated with a potential function $f,$ we compute its gradient.

$$
\begin{aligned}∇f & =\frac{∂f}{∂x}\,i+\frac{∂f}{∂y}\,j \\  & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1))\,i+\frac{∂}{∂y}(x\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1))\,j \\  & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1)\,i+\frac{2xy}{{y}^{2}+1}\,j \\  & =F\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the vector field that has $f$ as a potential function is

$$
F=\operatorname{ln}⁡({y}^{2}+1)\,i+\frac{2xy}{{y}^{2}+1}\,j.
$$

question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\text{div}\,F=∇\cdot F$ denotes the divergence of the vector field $F.$

Intuitively, the divergence of $F$ at a point $P$ measures how much $F$ acts like a source or a sink at $P:$

- If $F$ acts like a source at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F>0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F<0$ at $P.$

- If $F$ acts like neither a source nor a sink at $P,$ then $∇\cdot F=0$ at $P.$

![](images/6c/6c747149618d4c5ef35e727af15cd001365bd9c2d5e064689baf24c6ee23cff9.png)

If $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere in the domain of $F,$ we say that $F$ is solenoidal.

With that in mind, let's examine each statement:

- Statement $\text{div}\,F=0$ is true, whereas statements $\text{div}\,F>0$ and $\text{div}\,F<0$ are false. For any point $P,$ the sum of the inward-pointing vectors equals the sum of the outward-pointing vectors. Therefore, $F$ acts neither like a source nor a sink.

- Statement “$F$ is solenoidal” is true. Since $∇\cdot F=0$ everywhere, the vector field $F$ is solenoidal.

Therefore, the correct answer is $\text{div}\,F=0$; “$F$ is solenoidal” only.

question.:question/worked-solution:
Recall that $\text{curl}\,F$ denotes the curl of the vector field $F.$

To understand intuitively whether a vector field has a curl at a point $P$, imagine that our vector field $F$ represents the velocity field of a stream of flowing water. We place a paddlewheel at $P$ with the axis of rotation pointing in the $z$-direction, and we note whether the paddlewheel rotates or not.

- If the paddlewheel is forced to rotate due to the action of the water, then the vector field has curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- If the paddlewheel does not rotate due to the action of the water, then the velocity field has zero curl, i.e., $\text{curl}\,F=0.$

![](images/86/86aee33cdfa96ac0a61468cc9657e791e399f31c024cdbc3a932193dc897d534.png)

If $\text{curl}\,F=0$ everywhere in ${R}^{3}$, we say that $F$ is irrotational.

With that in mind, let's check each statement:

- Statement $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0$ is true, whereas statement $\text{curl}\,F=0$ is false. If a paddlewheel were placed at any point $P$ in the manner described above, it would rotate clockwise. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0.$

- Statement “$\text{curl}\,F$ points in the positive $z$-direction” is true. Using our right hand, if we wrap our fingers in the direction of rotation (counterclockwise), our thumb will point away from the screen. Therefore, $\text{curl}\,F$ also points away from the screen, in the direction of increasing $z.$

- Statement “$F$ is irrotational” is false. Since $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0,$ the vector field $F$ is not irrotational.

Therefore, the correct answer is $\text{curl}\,F\ne 0$; “$\text{curl}\,F$ points in the positive $z$-direction” only.
